title: Pulled satin stitch
subtitle: Rows of firm satin stitches pulled tight to open a mesh of holes in the weave
excerpt: Pulled satin stitch is a pulled-thread filling worked on evenweave fabric. Straight satin stitches are laid in rows over a counted number of threads and drawn firmly so the fabric threads are displaced sideways, opening small holes between each stitch. The pattern of holes gives the filling its lacy, openwork appearance rather than the thread covering it.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), pulled thread and whitework chapters. Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), drawn fabric and satin stitch entries.

content.text: Pulled satin stitch is not the same as ordinary satin stitch, though both use straight parallel stitches. In ordinary satin stitch the aim is to cover the fabric smoothly; in pulled satin stitch the aim is to displace the fabric threads so they cluster apart from each other and leave holes. The thread used is fine and matches the fabric in colour, making it nearly invisible. The visible pattern is entirely the mesh of openings. The stitch is worked over a counted number of fabric threads on evenweave, with a blunt tapestry needle so the fabric threads are separated cleanly and not pierced.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Coton a broder no. 16 or 25, or a single strand of stranded cotton, in a shade matching the fabric; the thread should almost disappear into the weave

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Evenweave linen or cotton, 28 to 32 count; the weave must be regular so pulled holes appear at consistent intervals. Work over 4 fabric threads per stitch

items.label: Needle
items.value: Tapestry needle size 24 or 26 (blunt); essential to avoid splitting the ground threads

items.label: Hoop
items.value: Rigid slate frame or 20 cm hoop; the fabric must be taut so every stitch pulls against a firm surface

content.text: Secure the thread on the back in the solid fabric outside the filling area. Bring the needle up at point (A) at the top of the first stitch position. Count 4 fabric threads downward and insert the needle at point (B). Pull the thread firmly and evenly so it tightens into the weave without snapping.

Bring the needle up at point (C), immediately beside (A) (one fabric thread to the right, or as set by the stitch spacing). Insert again 4 threads below at (D), pulling firmly. Continue in this way across the row, placing stitches side by side over the same 4-thread height. Keep the tension identical on every stitch.

At the end of the row, bring the needle up 4 threads below the base of the last stitch to begin the next row. Work back in the opposite direction, placing stitches in the same columns so the base of each stitch in the upper row shares a hole with the top of the corresponding stitch below. This shared-hole arrangement increases the hole size and is key to the openwork effect.

Continue filling the shape in rows, keeping the stitch count and pull tension uniform throughout. The filling should look like an even net of small holes when held up to the light. Fasten off on the back.

attrs.heading: When pulled satin stitch goes wrong

items.symptom: The holes are inconsistent: some are large and some barely visible
items.cause: Tension varied across stitches, or the stitches are not sharing holes correctly between rows.
items.fix: Pull every stitch with the same deliberate force. Check that the base of each stitch in a row lands exactly in the same hole as the top of the stitch below it in the next row. If holes at shared points are missing, the rows are offset.

items.symptom: The fabric puckers and distorts after working
items.cause: The overall tension is too strong and uneven, or the fabric was not mounted taut enough.
items.fix: Use a rigid frame rather than a hoop if distortion is severe. Firm, even tension is the goal; yanking the thread tight enough to deform the whole fabric is too much.

items.symptom: Thread shows prominently across the surface
items.cause: The thread is too thick or too contrasting in colour.
items.fix: Use the finest thread that allows firm pulling without breaking, in a shade as close to the fabric as possible. Pulled satin stitch should read as texture, not thread.

content.text: Pulled satin stitch is a standard filling for whitework. It is common in Hardanger and Scandinavian work, where it fills the solid areas between cut sections. It uses the same formation as
